items.title: The Economics of Environmental Degradation
items.body:
### Why the economy harms the environment

**In one line**
Environmental degradation is the wearing-down of nature — forests, air, water, soil and wildlife — and economists explain it as the market quietly failing to charge anyone for the damage.

**Why it is asked**
Prelims tests the four forms of degradation and the three market-failure ideas (externality, commons, Kuznets curve); Mains asks you to use them to argue 'why does growth pollute, and what can fix it'.

**The story**
Think of a factory beside a river. It pays for labour, power and raw material — its **private cost**. But it also dumps waste into the river, and the villagers downstream pay for that in illness and lost fishing. That extra, unpaid burden on outsiders is the **social cost**. Because the factory never pays it, its goods look cheap, so it makes **more** of them than is good for society — this is a **negative externality**, and it is the heart of why markets harm the environment.

Clean air and a stable climate are **public goods**: no one can be shut out of them and one person breathing clean air does not use it up, so no business can sell them and markets under-supply them. Shared, unowned resources — a village grazing ground, an ocean fishery — face the **tragedy of the commons** (named by Garrett Hardin in 1968): each herder adds one more cow because the gain is his alone while the cost of overgrazing is split among all, so everyone over-uses the resource until it collapses.

A hopeful twist is the **Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC)** — an inverted-U. Poor countries pollute little; as they industrialise, pollution rises; but once they are rich enough, citizens demand clean air and can afford clean technology and strong laws, so pollution falls again.

**Picture it**

| Form of degradation | Everyday example |
|---|---|
| Deforestation | Clearing forest for farms or mines |
| Air / water / soil pollution | Factory smoke, river effluent, chemical run-off |
| Soil degradation & desertification | Over-farming turning fertile land barren |
| Loss of biodiversity | Species dying out as habitats vanish |

**Terms explained**
- **Externality** — a cost (or benefit) that falls on someone outside the deal who was never paid or charged for it.
- **Private cost vs social cost** — what the producer pays versus what society as a whole pays; pollution makes social cost the larger of the two.
- **Public good** — something non-excludable (no one can be kept out) and non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's), like clean air.
- **Common-pool resource** — rival (it can be used up) but non-excludable (hard to fence off), like a fishery.

**Don't confuse**
- A **public good** (clean air — non-rival) is not the same as a **common-pool resource** (a fishery — rival but open to all).
- The **Environmental** Kuznets Curve (income versus pollution) is different from Simon Kuznets' original curve (income versus inequality).

**Remember it**
Degradation has four forms — **'DPSB': D**eforestation, **P**ollution, **S**oil/desertification, **B**iodiversity loss — and markets fail because nobody is billed for the harm.

**TL;DR**

| Idea | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Negative externality | Producer does not pay the harm, so social cost > private cost and the dirty good is over-made |
| Public good | Clean air cannot be sold, so markets under-provide it |
| Tragedy of the commons (Hardin 1968) | Everyone over-uses a shared, unowned resource |
| Environmental Kuznets Curve | Pollution rises with income, then falls after a turning point (inverted-U) |
keyPoints: Main forms of degradation: deforestation, pollution (air/water/soil), soil degradation/desertification, biodiversity loss.
A negative externality means social cost exceeds private cost, causing overproduction of the polluting good.
Tragedy of the commons (Hardin, 1968): open-access shared resources are overused.
Environmental Kuznets Curve is an inverted-U between per-capita income and degradation.
Environmental goods fail in markets because they are externalities, public goods or common-pool resources.
items.mnemonic: Degradation = 'DPSB' — Deforestation, Pollution, Soil/desertification, Biodiversity loss.
items.source: NCERT Introductory Microeconomics; Britannica — externalities, commons, EKC

items.title: Environmental Policy Instruments & Principles
items.body:
### How governments correct pollution

**In one line**
Once we accept that pollution is an unpaid cost, policy fixes it two ways — by ordering firms what they may emit (command-and-control) or by putting a price on pollution so firms choose to cut it (market-based).

**Why it is asked**
Examiners love the contrast between the two toolkits, the exact meaning of a Pigouvian tax and cap-and-trade, and the two principles (Polluter Pays, Precautionary) the Supreme Court made part of Indian law.

**The story**
Suppose the state wants a steel plant to pollute less. Under **command-and-control** it simply issues a rule: 'emit no more than X, or lose your licence.' This is direct and certain, but one-size-fits-all — a clean firm and a dirty firm face the same rule, and neither is rewarded for doing better.

Under a **market-based** approach the state instead makes pollution cost money. A **Pigouvian tax** charges the firm a tax equal to the exact harm each extra tonne of pollution causes (the marginal external cost); now the firm's private cost rises to the true social cost and it voluntarily cuts back. **Cap-and-trade** sets one total cap on emissions, hands out or auctions permits adding up to that cap, and lets firms buy and sell them — so cuts happen first where they are cheapest. The **Coase theorem** adds a third insight: if property rights are clear and bargaining is cheap, the two sides can simply negotiate a clean outcome without any government at all.

Underpinning all of this are two principles the Supreme Court read into the right to life (**Article 21**): the **Polluter Pays Principle** (whoever causes the pollution pays to clean it up) and the **Precautionary Principle** (if an activity might cause serious harm, you act to prevent it even before the science is 100% certain).

**Picture it**

| Toolkit | Examples | Core idea |
|---|---|---|
| Command-and-control | Emission standards, bans, licensing, EIA clearance | The state dictates how much may be emitted |
| Market-based | Pigouvian tax, cap-and-trade, clean-tech subsidies | The state prices pollution and lets firms choose |

**Terms explained**
- **Pigouvian tax** — a tax set equal to the damage one extra unit of pollution causes, named after economist A.C. Pigou.
- **Marginal external cost** — the harm to outsiders from producing just one more unit.
- **Cap-and-trade** — a fixed overall emissions limit, with tradable permits beneath it.
- **Coase theorem** — the result that clear ownership plus cheap bargaining can solve pollution privately.
- **Sustainable development** — meeting present needs without robbing future generations (the Brundtland definition).

**Don't confuse**
- **Pigouvian tax** fixes the *price* of pollution and lets the quantity adjust; **cap-and-trade** fixes the *quantity* (the cap) and lets the price adjust.
- **Polluter Pays** (you pay for harm you cause) is different from the **Precautionary Principle** (act early under uncertainty).

**Remember it**
Two toolkits — **'CAC' (Command-And-Control) rules** versus **market prices (tax or trade)** — both anchored in Polluter Pays and Precaution.

**TL;DR**

| Instrument / principle | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Command-and-control | Government orders the emission limit |
| Pigouvian tax | Tax = the exact harm per unit, so firms internalise it |
| Cap-and-trade | Cap total emissions, trade permits, cut where cheapest |
| Coase theorem | Clear rights + cheap bargaining = efficiency, no state needed |
| Polluter Pays / Precaution | Read into Article 21 in the Vellore Citizens case, 1996 |
keyPoints: Policy instruments split into command-and-control (standards, bans, EIA) and market-based (Pigouvian tax, cap-and-trade, subsidies).
A Pigouvian tax equals the marginal external cost; cap-and-trade caps total emissions and allows permit trading.
Coase theorem: clear property rights + low bargaining cost can yield efficiency without regulation.
Polluter Pays and Precautionary principles are part of Indian law via Article 21 (Vellore Citizens case, 1996).
Sustainable development (Brundtland) balances present needs with future generations.
items.mnemonic: Two toolkits: 'CAC' (Command-And-Control) rules vs market prices (tax/trade).
items.source: NCERT; Supreme Court — Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996)

items.title: Environmental Laws, Institutions & EIA
items.body:
### India's environmental laws and watchdogs

**In one line**
India protects the environment through a chain of laws passed from 1972 onwards, a set of institutions that enforce them, and a clearance process (EIA) that screens big projects before they are built.

**Why it is asked**
The exact year of each law and the order in which they came are classic Prelims matching questions; the EIA stages and the EPA 1986 as the 'umbrella' law are recurring favourites.

**The story**
India's green laws were built one layer at a time. The **Wildlife Protection Act (1972)** came first, protecting species and creating sanctuaries. The **Water Act (1974)** followed and set up the **Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)** and the State Boards to police pollution. The **Forest Conservation Act (1980)** made it hard to divert forest land to other uses, and the **Air Act (1981)** extended pollution control to the air. Then came the turning point: the **1984 Bhopal Gas Tragedy** shocked the country, and in its wake Parliament passed the **Environment (Protection) Act, 1986** — an **umbrella law** giving the Centre sweeping power to set standards, restrict industries and issue directions.

To run all this, the **Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC)** is the nodal body; **CPCB and the State Boards** set and enforce standards; and the **National Green Tribunal (NGT), set up in 2010**, is a special court for fast environmental justice.

Before a large project (a dam, mine or factory) is cleared, it must pass an **Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)** under the **EIA Notification, 2006**. Big 'Category A' projects are judged by the MoEFCC's Expert Appraisal Committee; smaller 'Category B' projects by the State authority (SEIAA). The process has four steps and includes a public hearing so affected people can object.

**Picture it**

| Law | Year | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Wildlife Protection Act | 1972 | Protected areas & species |
| Water Act | 1974 | Created CPCB & State Boards |
| Forest Conservation Act | 1980 | Restricts diversion of forest land |
| Air Act | 1981 | Air-quality control |
| Environment (Protection) Act | 1986 | Umbrella law, after Bhopal (1984) |

**Terms explained**
- **Umbrella law** — a broad parent law under which the government can issue many detailed rules and notifications.
- **CPCB / SPCB** — Central / State Pollution Control Boards, the agencies that set and enforce pollution standards.
- **NGT** — National Green Tribunal, a dedicated court for environmental cases.
- **EIA** — Environmental Impact Assessment, a study of a project's likely environmental effects before approval.
- **SEIAA** — State Environment Impact Assessment Authority, which clears Category B projects.

**Don't confuse**
- The **Water Act is 1974** and the **Air Act is 1981** — easy to swap; the Water Act (not the Air Act) created the CPCB.
- **Category A** = central clearance (MoEFCC); **Category B** = state clearance (SEIAA).

**Remember it**
Law order **'72-74-80-81-86'** = Wildlife, Water, Forest, Air, Environment (the last being the umbrella Act after Bhopal).

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| EPA 1986 | The umbrella law, passed after Bhopal (1984) |
| CPCB | Created by the Water Act, 1974 |
| NGT | The green court, set up in 2010 |
| EIA (2006) | Four stages — Screening, Scoping, Public Consultation, Appraisal |
keyPoints: Chronology: Wildlife 1972, Water 1974, Forest Conservation 1980, Air 1981, EPA 1986 (umbrella, post-Bhopal).
The Water Act 1974 created the CPCB and State Pollution Control Boards.
NGT was established in 2010 for speedy disposal of environmental cases.
EIA is governed by the 2006 Notification under the EPA 1986, with Category A (central) and B (state) projects.
EIA stages: Screening, Scoping, Public Consultation, Appraisal.
items.mnemonic: Law order '72-74-80-81-86' = Wildlife, Water, Forest, Air, Environment.
items.source: MoEFCC — environmental legislation; EIA Notification 2006; NGT Act 2010

items.title: India's Climate Commitments — Paris, Panchamrit & Net-Zero
items.body:
### What India has promised on climate

**In one line**
Under the Paris Agreement India has made a set of climate promises — an updated 2022 target, five 'Panchamrit' pledges for 2030, and net-zero by 2070 — backed by missions and institutions.

**Why it is asked**
The five Panchamrit numbers, the 2070 net-zero year and the 2022 NDC figures are among the most-asked current-affairs facts in both Prelims and Mains.

**The story**
The **Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015)** asked every country to set its own climate pledge, called a **Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC)**, to keep global warming well below 2°C. India **updated its NDC in 2022** with two headline numbers: cut the **emissions intensity of GDP by 45%** by 2030 (against the 2005 level — up from the earlier 33–35%), and get **about 50%** of its electric power capacity from **non-fossil** sources by 2030 (up from 40%).

At **COP26 (Glasgow, 2021)** the Prime Minister announced the **Panchamrit** — literally 'five nectars' — five pledges, four of them for 2030 and the fifth a long-term goal: 500 GW of non-fossil power capacity, 50% of energy from renewables, a 45% cut in carbon intensity, a one-billion-tonne cut in projected emissions, and **net-zero by 2070**. 'Net-zero' does not mean zero emissions — it means whatever is still emitted is balanced by removals (forests, carbon capture). India chose 2070, later than the West's 2050, arguing that its historical and per-person emissions are low and it still needs room to grow.

Delivering this rests on an **architecture** built earlier: the **National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC, 2008)** with its **eight missions**, the **International Solar Alliance** (co-founded by India and France), and **Mission LiFE (2022)**, which nudges ordinary people toward low-carbon lifestyles.

**Picture it**

| Panchamrit pledge (by 2030 unless noted) | Value |
|---|---|
| Non-fossil capacity | 500 GW |
| Renewables in energy mix | 50% |
| Cut in carbon intensity (vs 2005) | 45% |
| Cut in projected emissions | 1 billion tonnes |
| Net-zero | 2070 |

**Terms explained**
- **NDC** — Nationally Determined Contribution, a country's own climate pledge under the Paris Agreement.
- **Emissions intensity of GDP** — greenhouse gases emitted per rupee of output; cutting it lets emissions fall per unit even as GDP grows.
- **Non-fossil capacity** — power-generating capacity from sources other than coal, oil and gas (solar, wind, hydro, nuclear).
- **Net-zero** — emissions left over are cancelled out by removals, giving a net of zero.
- **NAPCC** — National Action Plan on Climate Change, India's umbrella climate plan of eight missions.

**Don't confuse**
- **Net-zero by 2070** (a long-term goal) is NOT one of the four 2030 targets — it is the fifth, separate Panchamrit element.
- The **45% figure** is the cut in *carbon intensity*; the **50% figure** is the *non-fossil power* share — different targets, often swapped in options.

**Remember it**
Net-zero years run **'70-60-50'** — India 2070, China 2060, EU/US 2050.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Panchamrit (COP26, 2021) | 500 GW, 50% renewables, 45% intensity cut, 1 bn-tonne cut, net-zero 2070 |
| Updated NDC (2022) | 45% intensity cut + ~50% non-fossil power capacity by 2030 |
| NAPCC (2008) | India's umbrella plan of eight climate missions |
| ISA & Mission LiFE | India-France solar alliance; a push for green lifestyles |
keyPoints: India's net-zero target year is 2070 (fifth Panchamrit element, COP26 Glasgow 2021).
Updated NDC 2022: 45% cut in emissions intensity of GDP by 2030 (vs 2005) and ~50% non-fossil power capacity.
Panchamrit 2030 targets: 500 GW non-fossil capacity, 50% renewables, 45% intensity cut, 1 billion-tonne emission cut.
NAPCC (2008) has eight national missions, including the National Solar Mission.
International Solar Alliance was co-founded by India and France; Mission LiFE promotes sustainable lifestyles.
items.source: PIB / UNFCCC — Paris Agreement, India's updated NDC (2022), COP26 Panchamrit; MoEFCC — NAPCC

items.title: Carbon Markets & Green Finance in India
items.body:
### Pricing carbon and funding the green transition

**In one line**
A carbon market lets firms buy and sell the right to emit so that pollution is cut at the lowest cost, while green finance raises money specifically for environment-friendly projects.

**Why it is asked**
The Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS 2023), its parent Act and administrator, and India's first Sovereign Green Bonds are high-value current-affairs facts, often set as multi-statement questions.

**The story**
Imagine the government decides the whole economy may emit only a fixed amount of carbon. It hands each big factory a quota. A factory that cleans up easily will have spare quota; one that finds cleaning hard can **buy** that spare quota instead. Both sides gain, and the cheapest cuts happen first — that is a **carbon market**. Markets come in two types: **compliance** markets, where the law forces firms to meet targets, and **voluntary** markets, where firms buy credits by choice (for their image or CSR).

India's own market is the **Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), 2023**, notified under the **Energy Conservation Act, 2001 (amended 2022)**. The **Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE)** administers it and the **Grid Controller of India** runs the registry. It has two arms — a **compliance mechanism** (emission-intensity targets for obligated industries) and an **offset mechanism** (voluntary projects) — and the traded unit is the **Carbon Credit Certificate (CCC)**. This did not appear from nowhere: it builds on two older schemes, **PAT ('Perform, Achieve, Trade')**, which rewards energy-saving factories with tradable **ESCerts**, and **Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs)**, which capture the 'green' value of renewable power.

Separately, the government must *fund* clean projects. **Green finance** does this: India issued its first **Sovereign Green Bonds in 2022-23 (₹16,000 crore)** to pay for solar, wind, clean transport and tree-planting; **green budgeting** tags parts of the budget for environmental goals; and the **Green Credit Programme (2023)** rewards voluntary good deeds such as planting trees.

**Picture it**

| Instrument | What it is |
|---|---|
| CCTS 2023 (CCCs) | India's national carbon market, run by BEE |
| PAT (ESCerts) | Trade certificates for energy saved |
| REC | Certificate for the green attribute of renewable power |
| Sovereign Green Bond | Government loan raised to fund green projects |

**Terms explained**
- **Carbon credit** — a permit to emit one tonne of carbon-dioxide-equivalent; one credit = one tonne.
- **Compliance vs voluntary market** — mandatory (set by law) versus optional (bought by choice).
- **ESCerts** — Energy Saving Certificates earned by over-achieving factories under the PAT scheme.
- **Sovereign Green Bond** — government debt whose proceeds are ring-fenced for green projects.
- **Green budgeting** — using the budget's tagging and allocations to push environmental aims.

**Don't confuse**
- A carbon market moves money **between private firms**, NOT from the private sector to the State.
- **BRSR** sustainability disclosures are mandated by **SEBI** (not the RBI) for the top-1000 listed companies — a common exam trap.

**Remember it**
India's carbon-market lineage: **PAT (ESCerts) + REC → CCTS (Carbon Credit Certificates)**, all run by the BEE.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| CCTS 2023 | India's carbon market under the Energy Conservation Act, run by BEE |
| Two arms | Compliance (obligated industries) + offset (voluntary projects) |
| Sovereign Green Bonds | First issued 2022-23, worth ₹16,000 crore |
| Green Credit Programme (2023) | Rewards voluntary green actions such as tree-planting |
keyPoints: CCTS 2023 was notified under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001 (amended 2022); BEE is the administrator.
CCTS has a compliance mechanism (obligated entities) and an offset mechanism (voluntary projects).
Compliance carbon markets are mandatory; voluntary markets are by choice.
PAT scheme issues tradable ESCerts; RECs represent renewable-electricity attributes.
India issued its first Sovereign Green Bonds in 2022-23 (₹16,000 crore); the Green Credit Programme (2023) rewards voluntary green actions.
items.mnemonic: India's carbon-market lineage: PAT (ESCerts) + REC → CCTS (Carbon Credit Certificates).
items.source: Ministry of Power / BEE — CCTS 2023, PAT, REC; RBI — Sovereign Green Bonds; MoEFCC — Green Credit Programme

items.title: Green Accounting & Natural-Capital Accounting
items.body:
### Counting nature in the national accounts

**In one line**
Green accounting adjusts the usual measure of growth so that using up forests, water, minerals and clean air shows up as a loss, instead of being treated as free.

**Why it is asked**
The GDP-to-Green-GDP chain, the SEEA milestone years, and India's efforts (EnviStats, NCAVES, Dasgupta) are set as matching and multi-statement questions.

**The story**
Ordinary **GDP** adds up everything an economy produces, but it treats nature as a free gift. A country can cut down all its forests, sell the timber, and GDP goes **up** — even though the nation is poorer in a real sense. **Green accounting** fixes this blind spot by subtracting the cost of using up **natural capital**.

Start with GDP. Take away the wear-and-tear on machines and buildings (**depreciation of man-made capital**) and you get **Net Domestic Product (NDP)**. **Green GDP** goes one step further and also subtracts the depletion and degradation of **natural** capital. So the chain is: GDP → (minus man-made depreciation) → NDP → (minus natural-capital loss) → Green GDP.

To do this consistently, the UN built a global rulebook, the **System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA)**. Its lineage goes back to a **1993 handbook** attached to the System of National Accounts; its **Central Framework became an international standard in 2012**, and **SEEA Ecosystem Accounting followed in 2021**.

India has acted on all this. **MoSPI** has published **'EnviStats India' every year since 2018** using SEEA. India was a partner country in the **EU-UN NCAVES project (2017-21)** on ecosystem accounting. An **Expert Group under Sir Partha Dasgupta (2013)** gave India a Green National Accounts framework, and the global **Dasgupta Review (2021)** argued that the economy sits *inside* nature, not above it. **Uttarakhand** has moved to estimate its own **Gross Environment Product (GEP)**.

**Picture it**

| Aggregate | What is subtracted |
|---|---|
| GDP | Nothing — total output |
| NDP | Depreciation of man-made (fixed) capital |
| Green GDP | Also the depletion/degradation of natural capital |

**Terms explained**
- **Natural capital** — the stock of nature (forests, water, minerals, air) that yields benefits over time.
- **Green GDP** — GDP adjusted downward for resource depletion and environmental damage.
- **SEEA** — the UN's statistical standard for linking environmental and economic data.
- **Ecosystem services** — the benefits nature gives us, grouped as provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment).
- **Adjusted Net Savings / Inclusive Wealth Index** — a World Bank and a UNEP measure, respectively, of whether a nation is truly saving once nature is counted.

**Don't confuse**
- **NDP** nets out only **man-made** capital's wear; **Green GDP** also nets out **natural** capital loss.
- **Green GDP** is an economy-wide adjustment — it is NOT the GDP of the renewable-energy sector, nor merely 'real' (inflation-adjusted) GDP.

**Remember it**
Green GDP = **NDP minus the loss of natural capital** — the greener the subtraction, the truer the growth.

**TL;DR**

| Point | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Green GDP | NDP minus depletion/degradation of natural capital |
| SEEA years | 1993 handbook, 2012 Central Framework, 2021 Ecosystem Accounting |
| EnviStats India | Published by MoSPI annually since 2018 |
| Dasgupta | India Expert Group 2013; global Dasgupta Review 2021 |
keyPoints: Green GDP = NDP minus depletion/degradation of natural capital; NDP already nets out fixed-capital depreciation.
SEEA Central Framework became a UN standard in 2012; SEEA Ecosystem Accounting in 2021; origin in the 1993 SNA handbook.
MoSPI publishes 'EnviStats India' annually since 2018 using the SEEA framework.
India was a partner country of the EU-UN NCAVES project (2017-21) on ecosystem accounting.
A Partha Dasgupta Expert Group gave India a Green National Accounts framework in 2013; the Dasgupta Review followed in 2021.
Uttarakhand moved to estimate its Gross Environment Product (GEP).
Adjusted Net Savings (World Bank) and the Inclusive Wealth Index (UNEP) are allied natural-capital indicators.
Ecosystem services: provisioning, regulating, cultural and supporting (Millennium Ecosystem Assessment).
items.source: UN SEEA; MoSPI — EnviStats India; World Bank; UNEP; HM Treasury — Dasgupta Review (2021)

items.title: For Mains — Environmental Degradation & Policy
items.body:
### For Mains — how to argue environment questions

Mains Paper-5 (clauses M5-5 and M5-6) asks about the **development-versus-environment trade-off, pollution and resource depletion, global environmental legislation and the SDGs**. The economic framing from this subtopic is your sharpest tool: treat degradation as **market failure** and policy as the correction.

**Dimensions the examiner expects**

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Diagnosis | Pollution as a negative externality; commons; public goods; undervalued natural capital |
| Instruments | Command-and-control vs market-based (Pigouvian tax, cap-and-trade); Coase |
| India's response | CCTS 2023, Sovereign Green Bonds, Green Credit Programme, NAPCC, Mission LiFE |
| Global architecture | Paris 2015, Kyoto, CITES, Montreal Protocol, SDGs, REDD+ |
| Criticism / limits | Coal dependence, finance & technology gaps, weak EIA enforcement, EKC not automatic for CO2 |
| Way forward | Just transition, green finance scale-up, natural-capital accounting in budgets |

**Data points, reports and judgments to quote**
- Panchamrit (COP26, 2021): 500 GW non-fossil, 50% renewables, 45% intensity cut, 1 bn-tonne cut, net-zero 2070.
- Updated NDC 2022: 45% emissions-intensity cut, ~50% non-fossil power by 2030.
- Sovereign Green Bonds 2022-23 (₹16,000 crore); CCTS 2023 under the Energy Conservation Act (BEE).
- Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India (1996) — Polluter Pays & Precautionary principles into Article 21.
- Dasgupta Review (2021) — 'the economy is embedded within nature'; MoSPI EnviStats India (since 2018).

**Use in answers**
- **Example:** cite the CCTS as India moving from command-and-control to market-based pricing of carbon.
- **Quote:** 'We are the trustees, not the owners, of the planet' — frame net-zero 2070 through climate justice and common-but-differentiated responsibilities.
- **Diagram idea:** draw the inverted-U Environmental Kuznets Curve, or the GDP → NDP → Green GDP subtraction chain, to show you can model the trade-off, not just describe it.
- **AP angle (where natural):** link to Andhra Pradesh's 160 GW green-energy-by-2047 ambition and the Harita AP green-cover target (30% by Jan 2026, 50% by 2047) as a state applying the national framework.
keyPoints: Frame environment answers as market failure (externalities, commons, undervalued natural capital) corrected by regulation and pricing.
Quote Panchamrit, the 2022 NDC, CCTS 2023 and Sovereign Green Bonds as India's response.
Cite the Vellore Citizens case (Polluter Pays/Precautionary into Article 21) and the Dasgupta Review (2021).
Balance with criticism — coal dependence, finance/technology gaps, weak EIA enforcement, EKC not automatic for CO2.
Use the EKC inverted-U or the GDP-NDP-Green GDP chain as a diagram; add the AP green-energy/Harita AP angle.
items.source: PIB/UNFCCC — Panchamrit & NDC; Ministry of Power — CCTS 2023; HM Treasury — Dasgupta Review (2021); AP Budget 2026-27 (PRS)
